opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that experience stuck with me. When you're in high school and you've poured months into something, you assume that effort translates into results. Then it doesn't work, and the first instinct is to think you weren't cut out for it, or that you picked the wrong problem.

What Johannes helped me see was that a setback in research is mostly information. It tells you something about the problem, or your approach, or your assumptions. It isn't a verdict on you. He was very calm about it, almost matter-of-fact: okay, this didn't work, so what did we learn, and what's the next thing to try? Watching someone more experienced treat failure as normal changed how I related to it.

The bigger lesson for me was that persistence isn't stubbornly repeating the same thing. It's staying committed to the goal while being flexible about the path. You keep the ambition and change the approach. That's carried over into everything since. Building a company, especially in AI, is basically a long sequence of things not working until something does. If you take every failed experiment personally, you burn out quickly. If you see each one as a step toward the answer, you can keep going for years.

So I'm grateful it happened early. It's much easier to learn that lesson at sixteen, when the stakes are low, than for the first time when you're running a team and there's real money on the line.

r001.rationale: The response explains a lesson about persistence and adapting after failure, but does not say Steinberger continued the research while unsure he could succeed.

r002.rationale: It says the experience changed how he related to failure, but does not describe a lasting reduction in his self-doubt.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Johannes was a researcher at the university in Vienna, and I was maybe sixteen when I basically cold-emailed him and asked if he'd work with me. I had no business doing that, honestly, but he said yes. And the first real project we did together, I poured everything into it. I was coding at night, skipping things at school, reading papers I barely understood. And then we found out, pretty late, that someone else had already published essentially the same idea, and done it better. Months of work, and it just evaporated.

I remember being genuinely devastated. At that age you kind of think your first big attempt is going to define whether you're "good" or not. And Johannes was very calm about it. He said something like, this is just what research is. Most of what you do doesn't work, and some of what works gets scooped. The thing that matters is whether you're still doing it next year.

That reframed it for me completely. I stopped thinking of persistence as this heroic thing where you grit your teeth through pain, and started thinking of it as just the baseline cost of doing anything hard. If you expect ninety percent of your effort to lead nowhere, then a failure isn't a signal to quit, it's just Tuesday. And weirdly that made me far more willing to take on things that looked impossible, because I wasn't betting my self-worth on any single attempt anymore.

So later, when I was working on poker AI and getting beaten by much better-funded groups, or now with Magic where the whole premise sounds absurd to a lot of people, I draw on that. The setback didn't make me tougher in some dramatic way. It just made me realistic, and realistic turns out to be a lot more durable than tough.

r001.rationale: He says the setback taught him to keep doing research despite expecting most efforts to fail, and that he became more willing to take on work that looked impossible.

r002.rationale: He says the setback changed his outlook so he no longer bet his self-worth on any single attempt, describing a lasting shift toward greater realism and durability.

astra-6.text: It helped me separate a particular approach failing from the whole goal being impossible. When you’ve put a lot of effort into something, it’s tempting to take a setback as a verdict on whether you’re capable of doing the work. But in research, you’re trying things whose outcomes you don’t know. Persistence means being willing to look honestly at what didn’t work, change your approach, and try again. It doesn’t mean insisting that your first idea has to be right.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it taught me to separate an idea failing from me failing. When you’re starting out, you want the work to validate that you’re good at this. A setback can feel very personal. But research means trying things when you don’t know whether they’ll work.

The lesson I took from working with Johannes was to keep learning and keep going, without becoming attached to one particular approach. Persistence doesn’t mean repeating the same thing indefinitely. It means being willing to say, “Okay, that didn’t work. What did we learn, and what should we try next?”

r001.rationale: He says research involves trying things without knowing whether they will work, and that he kept learning and going after setbacks.
